title: Immunotherapy for Depression: New Trial Tests Tocilizumab (Actemra)
summary: A breakthrough trial tested immunotherapy for depression using the anti-inflammatory drug tocilizumab (Actemra). See the results and what they mean for treatment-resistant depression.
body_text: Tocilizumab (Actemra) for Depression: The Trial Tocilizumab , sold under the brand name Actemra, is a biologic drug that blocks the IL-6 receptor. It is FDA approved for inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, but it has never been an approved treatment for any mental health condition. The new trial tested whether it could become one. The University of Bristol-led study enrolled 30 adults with moderate to severe depression that had not responded to standard antidepressants. Importantly, every participant also showed signs of low-grade inflammation on blood testing, a selection strategy that set this trial apart from earlier research. Fourteen participants received a single intravenous infusion of tocilizumab, while sixteen received a saline placebo, and all were followed for four weeks. The results were notable for such a small study. In the tocilizumab group, 54% of participants achieved depression remission, compared to 31% in the placebo group. The number needed to treat was calculated at 5, meaning five people would need the treatment for one additional person to benefit. For context, that figure is around 7 for SSRIs , the most commonly prescribed antidepressants. Participants who received the drug also showed greater improvements in fatigue, quality of life, and anxiety measures. The researchers were careful to note the limitations of this trial. With only 30 participants, there was limited statistical evidence of major differences between groups, and the trial was designed as a proof of concept rather than a definitive test.

title: Jilin University Accelerates Student Racing Success Using Fidelity CFD Software
summary: Founded in 1955, the College of Automotive Engineering at Jilin University has a long tradition of developing automotive talent. That commitment extends beyond the classroom through its student racing program, established in 2007, which has become on...
body_text: Jilin University Accelerates Student Racing Success Using Fidelity CFD Software 21 Jul 2026 • 2 minute read Founded in 1955, the College of Automotive Engineering at Jilin University has a long tradition of developing automotive talent. That commitment extends beyond the classroom through its student racing program, established in 2007, which has become one of the most successful in China. In recent years, Jilin University's student racing teams have earned 16 national championship trophies, including record-setting victories in electric, hybrid, and energy-efficiency competitions. In 2024, Jilin University partnered with Cadence to establish the first joint computational fluid dynamics (CFD) laboratory at a Chinese university. The collaboration brought advanced simulation technologies into both engineering education and student motorsports programs, enabling students to work with professional-grade tools used throughout the automotive industry. For the university's racing teams, access to Cadence technology has been transformative. "Cadence not only provides us with professional CFD tools, but also gives us the opportunity to think like real engineers," said team members. Moving beyond theoretical calculations, students can now perform high-fidelity simulations that help them analyze, validate, and optimize designs before building physical prototypes. The impact was especially evident during preparation for the 2025 Formula SAE Japan competition. Using Cadence Fidelity CFD Software, the team completed more than 50 iterations of rear-wing designs. By analyzing static pressure contours and velocity vector fields, they identified flow separation issues and optimized the wing geometry. The result was a 23% increase in downforce, resulting in multiple awards, including Best Aerodynamic Design, Best Ergonomic Design, and Best CAE Simulation Application, and nine other special honors. Cadence tools have also supported the team's championship-winning Gspeed Future Vector hybrid racing car. Students used Fidelity simulations to optimize airflow channels, evaluate thermal management strategies, and improve vehicle-level integration. By identifying viable designs earlier in the development process, the team significantly reduced costly trial-and-error cycles. Beyond performance gains, simulation has improved productivity. According to the team, adopting Cadence Fidelity CFD tools reduced simulation workflow time by more than 60%, enabling faster design iterations and more efficient engineering decisions. As the partnership grows, Jilin University hopes to expand collaboration into emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, new energy technologies, and advanced materials. Together, Jilin University and Cadence are helping students develop the skills, experience, and engineering mindset needed to drive the next generation of automotive innovation. Learn more about how Jilin University is building award-winning race cars with Cadence . "Designed with Cadence" is a series of videos that showcases creative products and technologies that are accelerating industry innovation using Cadence tools and solutions. For more Designed with Cadence videos, check out the Cadence website and YouTube channel .

title: Top 5 des raisons pour lesquelles les vendeurs médias devraient se soucier du trafic non-humain et de la fraude publicitaire
summary: Il est dans l’intérêt de tous les vendeurs médias – aussi bien les éditeurs, les SSP (Supply Side Platforms) que les ad networks – de devancer les fraudeurs dans cette lutte pour protéger la réputation des marques médias.
body_text: Cet article est le troisième d’une série présentant les solutions pour combattre les problématiques liées à la fraude publicitaire, le trafic non-humain ainsi que la visibilité. Son but est d’expliquer l’impact que génèrent ces problématiques sur l’écosystème publicitaire et de présenter comment Comscore œuvre pour combattre ces freins à la progression de la publicité digitale, afin qu’acheteurs et vendeurs médias gardent une longueur d’avance sur les fraudeurs. Il est possible que certains soient fatigués d’entendre parler de fraude publicitaire, de visibilité ou encore de trafic non-humain au sein de l’écosystème digital. Après tout, avec tous ces nouveaux types de fraude dénoncés dans la presse, que reste-t-il à dire sur le sujet ? Et finalement, cette problématique de fraude publicitaire, ne concerne-t-elle pas uniquement les acheteurs médias, vu que ce sont eux qui en paient l’addition ? La vérité est plutôt qu’il y a encore beaucoup à dire sur le sujet et que les vendeurs sont tout aussi exposés que les acheteurs médias à ce fléau. Chaque technologie de fraude qui n’est pas encore identifiée est une menace potentielle pour votre marque en tant que vendeur média, pouvant compromettre vos revenus publicitaires. En clair, il est dans l’intérêt de tous les vendeurs médias – aussi bien les éditeurs, les SSP (Supply Side Platforms) que les ad networks – de devancer les fraudeurs dans cette lutte pour protéger la réputation des marques médias. Ci-dessous un Top 5, en ordre inversé dans un style purement emprunté à David Letterman, présentant les raisons pour lesquelles vous devriez placer la lutte contre le NHT en tête de vos priorités si vous êtes ou souhaitez être reconnu en tant qu’éditeur Premium : 5. Vos investissements : Chaque centime de revenu publicitaire allant à un opérateur de bot ou tout autre fraudeur est un centime de moins pour un vendeur média légitime. Pendant que les éditeurs Premium investissent dans leur média, les créateurs de NHT et autres fraudeurs détournent leurs revenus publicitaires et empêchent tout retour sur investissement. 4. Votre identité en tant qu’éditeur : L’une des formes de fraude publicitaire la plus répandue actuellement et souvent appelée blanchiment de domaine ou masquage d’URL, est littéralement le détournement de votre identité par un fraudeur. Un escroc fait croire qu’il possède votre contenu, vos publicités et votre audience en imitant vos URL sur les ad exchanges. Lorsqu’un acheteur paie pour acquérir cet inventaire en pensant qu’il s’agit de celui de votre média alors qu’en réalité il achète un nom de domaine “blanchi”, il obtient bien souvent des taux de couverture sur cible, de clics et d’engagement surréalistes à un prix très bas. Pire, dans certains cas, l’acheteur obtiendra des performances très basses qui auront pour conséquence de sévèrement ternir votre marque. Dans tous les cas, votre prochaine interaction avec cet acheteur, agence publicitaire ou annonceur, sera fortement impactée par l’expérience qu’il pense avoir eue avec vous alors qu’en réalité il s’agissait de blanchiment de domaine. Tel en est l'impact. 3. Votre audience : Le NHT empêche tout acheteur de différencier votre audience et votre marque Premium d’un générateur de bots ou de réseaux fantômes (‘ghost network’, technique de fraude fréquente impliquant la création de centaines voire de milliers de faux sites s’appropriant de manière illicite le contenu d’autres éditeurs et achetant du trafic de bots pour simuler les impressions de véritables internautes). Compte tenu de la tendance actuelle des acheteurs à “acheter des audiences partout” et non plus uniquement auprès d’éditeurs spécifiques, il est plus important que jamais de prouver la valeur de votre audience – réelle et composée de vraies personnes susceptibles d’être impactées par les publicités. C’est le seul moyen que vous ayez pour différencier votre marque. Après tout, si des impressions frauduleuses sur votre site sont considérées comme provenant de vrais humains, le ROI de la publicité sur votre média en sera déprécié, forçant les annonceurs à dévaluer votre inventaire et sa capacité à générer un impact conséquent. 2. Votre stratégie de croissance : Le discours autour de la fraude publicitaire et le NHT a fait de l’expression « acheter du trafic » un terme péjoratif. Mais il ne devrait pas en être ainsi. Tout comme les annonceurs, les éditeurs doivent être capables d’acquérir de nouveaux clients (utilisateurs et lecteurs de leurs sites) et évaluer les partenaires qui peuvent les aider à le faire. L’extension d’audience et l’acquisition de trafic ne sont pas des actions fondamentalement mauvaises, du moment que cela n’implique pas de fraude publicitaire. Mais pour que ce soit le cas, les éditeurs ont besoin d’outils pour vérifier les sources de trafic et éradiquer le NHT. 1. Votre carrière professionnelle et votre industrie : OK, même si cela peut donner l’impression d’être deux raisons en une, la vérité est que nous avons tous choisi de construire notre carrière dans la publicité digitale et ceci est un fait : si l’industrie n’est pas regardée d’un très bon œil, nous allons tous en pâtir. Les investissements en publicité ne seront pas alloués au digital aussi vite qu’ils le devraient, les innovations seront limitées (du fait que des technologies et entreprises légitimes ne pourront se développer car étouffées par la mauvaise herbe que représente le NHT). Il est donc plus difficile pour nous tous de nous lancer dans d’autres industries ou verticales lorsque nous venons d’un segment globalement mal vu. Lutter contre la fraude publicitaire affecte chacun d’entre nous personnellement et devrait être considéré autant comme une priorité professionnelle que personnelle. Alors quoi faire ? Surveiller le trafic sur vos inventaires – aussi bien sur site que hors-site – vous permettra de protéger la réputation de votre marque et vous empêchera de devenir l’une des victimes du NHT. Sans cela, vous êtes dans l’incapacité d’assurer et de maintenir la valeur de votre inventaire ainsi que de votre marque média. Vous compromettez votre capacité à répondre aux besoins des annonceurs en termes de couverture sur cible et de visibilité, mais également d’engagement humain et véritable qui permettra aux publicités d’avoir l’impact recherché. Une surveillance et une évaluation continues du trafic à l’aide de solutions avancées de mesure et d’identification du NHT est une réponse. Pour en savoir plus sur la façon dont le NHT affecte les éléments clés différenciant votre inventaire publicitaire et les solutions qui existent, téléchargez notre livret sur le Trafic Non-Humain . title: Why Better Tasting Rooms Start With Customer Data
summary: Customer data strategies for wineries from Awtomic CEO Emily Yuhas and WISE Winery Coach Liz Mercer. Learn how top-performing wineries use tasting room insights to build stronger customer relationships and wine clubs.
body_text: Most of the wineries I talk to (which is dozens every week) claim the thing that sets them apart from other wineries is their wine. Theirs is grown a special way on a special hill in a special part of the world. But according to Liz Mercer , Winery Coach, Content Developer, and Instructor at WISE , that's not what separates the wineries that are growing from the ones that are standing still. After helping educate winery teams, consulting with DTC leaders, and conducting nearly 7,000 mystery shops, Liz’s experience and recommendations follow one consistent pattern: The wineries seeing the most success have built a culture around customer data. "The number one distinguishing factor is they have a strong culture of data capture, and they do something with it. They're building their mailing lists and they're using their tasting room as a launchpad for a long-term relationship." So what happens when wineries emphasize learning, understanding, and treating the customer like a friend? In short, magic. Customers respond with higher lifetime value, lower churn, and overall satisfaction. Great Wineries Collect More and Better Data Ask most wineries what customer data they collect and you'll hear the basics. Name, email address, phone number, maybe a birthday. Liz actually jokes she'd be excited if every winery consistently captured ZIP code because even that isn't always happening. Without the basics, you can't continue the relationship after someone leaves your tasting room. But top-performing wineries don't stop there and Liz thinks about customer data in three layers. Level 1: Contact data This is the information that allows you to stay in touch with someone. Name Email Phone number SMS and email opt-in permission Birthday Address Level 2: Behavioral data This tells you how someone interacts with your winery. Purchases Tasting room visits Event attendance Wine club membership Favorite wines Referral activity Level 3: Relationship data Relationship data provides context. Who referred them? What other wine clubs do they belong to? Do they travel often? Are they local or destination visitors? Do they host guests at home frequently? Why did they visit your winery in the first place? Who did they attend with? Level one helps you contact a customer. Level two helps you understand their behavior. Level three helps you build an actual relationship. As Liz puts it, wineries need to move "beyond anecdotal to actionable." How to Train Your Tasting Room Team to Reveal Relationship Data Every day, guests tell wineries exactly how to build better relationships with them. One guest mentions they're visiting from out of state. Another says they're members at three other wineries. One group mentions they only make it to wine country once every few years. Those are opportunities to better understand your customers. The challenge is that too much of this information lives in employees' heads instead of your CRM. Liz believes wineries should intentionally train tasting room teams to uncover relationship data, understand why it matters, and consistently record it. That doesn't mean hospitality needs to turn into an interrogation. It means wineries are responsible for creating a culture where conversations become meaningful customer insights. I recognize that most wineries don't have perfectly built-out CRMs, robust training programs, or convenient places to record every customer insight. We're not working in a scientific lab, and the data capture process doesn't have to be perfect. What I consistently see among the wineries that are growing is a willingness to start anyway. They're finding creative ways to capture relationship data today because they understand its long-term value, even if the process is held together with a little duct tape. Every Useful Piece of Data Should Change What Happens Next If someone gives you their email address, the easiest solution is to add them to your monthly newsletter and move on. A better approach is to use every piece of information you've gathered to intentionally guide that customer into the right lifecycle flow. Someone who attended a winery event has a different relationship with your brand than someone who was referred by an existing wine club member. An event attendee may need more education about your winery before they're ready to join. A referred guest has already borrowed trust from someone who loves your brand so you may be able to skip some introductory messaging and instead recommend wines or membership benefits that align with what you already know about them. If a guest tells you they belong to three other wine clubs, ask why. What attracted them to those clubs? Which benefits do they actually use? That conversation can shape how you position your own membership, what benefits you emphasize, and even ideas for future improvements. During a personal trip, Liz told a winery she was visiting from across the country and likely wouldn't be back anytime soon. Instead of emphasizing shipping benefits, exclusive wines, or the convenience of membership from afar, the tasting room associate focused almost entirely on complimentary tastings, winery events, and bringing friends. The winery had the right data, they just didn't use it. The same principle applies everywhere: ZIP code : Segment local guests from destination visitors, promote nearby events, regional roadshows, pickup opportunities, or shipping benefits accordingly. Referral source : Strengthen relationships with hotels, concierges, existing members, creators, or local businesses that consistently send high-quality guests your way. Favorite wines : Recommend similar bottles, new releases, or club customizations that align with what they already enjoy. Purchase history : Someone who buys the same bottle of sparkling rosé every visit shouldn't receive the same recommendation as someone building a reserve wine collection. Visit frequency : Reward your regulars differently than someone who visits once every few years. Frequent guests may value member events and exclusive experiences, while infrequent visitors may need more digital touchpoints to stay connected. None of these data points are valuable on their own. Their value comes from changing what happens next. Turn Customer Data Into “Controlled Chaos" One of Liz's favorite concepts is what she calls "controlled chaos." Rather than overwhelming customers with endless choices, wineries should use customer data to confidently guide people toward the right experience. Instead of asking, "Would you like to take anything home today?" Try, "You mentioned you really enjoyed the Reserve Chardonnay and the single-vineyard Pinot Noir. How many bottles can I set you up with?" The same philosophy applies to memberships. You likely don't need six different club structures with dozens of benefits. You need a few clear options that staff understand well enough to confidently recommend based on what they've learned about the guest. Technology can surface purchase history, preferences, and customer attributes, but your staff still provides the judgment. Together, they create a much better customer experience. Better Data Creates Better Relationships The wineries seeing the most growth don't think of guests as people moving through a tasting room. They think of every tasting as the launchpad for a long-term relationship. Data isn't collected because your CRM needs another field filled out. It's collected so your next email feels more personal, your next text message is more relevant, and your next membership conversation is more helpful. Technology makes that easier, but technology isn't what creates memorable hospitality. People do. The wineries that continue to grow will be the ones that consistently collect the right information, empower their teams to use it, and make every interaction a little more personal than the last.

title: Best Free Headless CMS Platforms in 2026 (Ranked and Compared)
summary: Looking for a free headless CMS? We ranked the best platforms by what their free plans actually include: objects, API calls, team members, and upgrade paths. Cosmic leads the list.
body_text: If you're evaluating headless CMS platforms, the free plan is usually where the decision starts. You want to build something real, validate your architecture, and make sure the developer experience is solid before committing to a paid tier. The problem: free plans vary wildly. Some give you a genuinely useful starting point. Others are barely enough to run a demo. And a few popular platforms don't list Cosmic at all on their comparison pages, even though Cosmic's free plan stacks up well against the field. This post fixes that. We ranked the best free headless CMS platforms in 2026 by what you actually get on the free tier: content objects, API access, team members, and a realistic upgrade path. What to look for in a free headless CMS Before the rankings, here's what actually matters on a free plan: Objects / content entries: how much content can you store before hitting a wall? API access: can you actually build a production-ready app, or are you rate-limited out of the gate? Team members: can more than one person use the free plan? Buckets / workspaces: can you run more than one project? Upgrade path: when you outgrow free, does the next tier make sense for your team size and budget? AI features: does the platform give you any AI tooling on free, or lock it behind enterprise? The best free headless CMS platforms in 2026 1. Cosmic Free plan includes: 1 Bucket (project) 2 Team members 1,000 Objects REST API + JavaScript/TypeScript SDK Media storage and imgix image optimization 1 AI Agent (draft, publish, and manage content from Slack, WhatsApp, or Telegram) Full dashboard access Cosmic's free plan is genuinely useful for small projects and solo developers, and it's the only free plan in this list that includes an AI Agent out of the box. You can connect a Slack channel and have an AI Agent draft, edit, and publish content without touching the dashboard at all. The REST API and TypeScript SDK are fully available on free, so you can build a real production app without hitting artificial API rate limits. When you're ready to grow, the Builder plan ($49/month) gives you 2 Buckets, 3 Team members, 5,000 Objects, and 3 AI Agents. No dramatic price jump, and the upgrade path maps directly to real team growth. Best for: solo developers, lean startup teams, anyone who wants AI-native content tooling from day one. Start free on Cosmic | See all plans 2. Contentful Free plan includes: 10 Team members 2 roles, 2 locales 25 Content types 100,000 API calls/month 50GB CDN bandwidth/month 10,000 records 1 Starter Space Contentful's free plan is generous on team seats (10 users), which makes it appealing for larger teams just starting out. The 100k API call limit is enough for prototyping but can become a constraint on a high-traffic production site. The bigger limitation: Contentful's paid plans start at $300/month (Lite), which is a significant jump once you need more locales, roles, or API capacity. Best for: larger teams who want to prototype with headless CMS before committing to a budget. 3. Sanity Free plan includes: Up to 20 users Unlimited content types 1M API CDN requests/month 250,000 API requests/month 100GB asset storage 100GB bandwidth 2 datasets Sanity's free tier is genuinely generous on users and API calls. The GROQ query language gives developers fine-grained control over content fetching. The tradeoff: Sanity has a steeper learning curve than most CMS platforms, and the free plan limits you to 2 datasets (projects). Sanity Studio (the editing interface) requires configuration that's less approachable for non-technical editors. Best for: developers comfortable with a code-first CMS who want flexibility on content modeling. 4. Strapi Free plan includes: Self-hosted (open source) Unlimited users Unlimited content types REST and GraphQL API Community support only Strapi is open source, so the software itself is free. But "free" here means you're managing your own hosting, security, backups, and updates. For a small team without dedicated DevOps resources, that's a real operational cost. Strapi Cloud (managed) starts at $29/month, which removes the self-hosting burden but adds a recurring cost. Best for: developers who want full control and are comfortable self-hosting. 5. Storyblok Free plan includes: 1 user 1 locale 200 components 100,000 API calls/month 1TB asset storage Storyblok's free plan is limited to a single user, which makes it essentially a solo-developer or personal-project tier. The 1TB asset storage is generous, but the 1-user cap means even a two-person team needs a paid plan. Storyblok's visual editor is its standout feature, but it's most valuable for content editors, who you can't add on free. Best for: solo developers evaluating Storyblok's visual editing experience. 6. Prismic Free plan includes: 1 user 1 locale Unlimited documents 4M API calls/month Page builder Prismic's free plan has the highest API call limit in the group (4M/month), which is more than enough for any production project at the free tier. Like Storyblok, the 1-user cap is the main constraint. The page builder is included on free, which is a genuine differentiator for marketing teams who want visual editing without code. Best for: solo developers or marketers who want high API throughput and a visual page builder. 7. Hygraph Free plan includes: 3 seats 2 roles 2 locales 10 components 500,000 API calls/month Unlimited asset storage Comments and live preview Hygraph's Hobby plan is one of the more collaborative free tiers in the group, with 3 seats, commenting, and live preview included. It's GraphQL-native, which is a strength for developers who want a flexible query layer but a constraint if your stack doesn't lean that way. The 10-component limit can become a bottleneck on more complex content models. Best for: small teams who want collaborative features and GraphQL on a free plan. Free plan comparison at a glance Cosmic: 2 team members, 1 Bucket, 1,000 Objects, full REST API + SDK, 1 AI Agent Contentful: 10 users, 2 locales, 100k API calls/month, 10,000 records Sanity: 20 users, 2 datasets, 1M API CDN requests/month, 100GB storage Strapi: unlimited users (self-hosted), no managed hosting on free Storyblok: 1 user, 1 locale, 100k API calls/month, 1TB storage Prismic: 1 user, 1 locale, 4M API calls/month Hygraph: 3 seats, 2 locales, 500k API calls/month, unlimited storage Which free headless CMS is right for you? Choose Cosmic if: you want AI-native content tooling from day one, a clean REST API and TypeScript SDK, and a free plan that covers real solo or two-person projects. The AI Agent inclusion on free is genuinely unique in this list. Choose Contentful if: you have a larger team (up to 10) who need to prototype together before committing to a budget. Choose Sanity if: you're a developer who wants maximum flexibility on content modeling and is comfortable with a code-first setup. The 20-user free tier is exceptionally generous. Choose Strapi if: you want full ownership and control and have the DevOps resources to self-host. Choose Storyblok or Prismic if: you're a solo developer and visual editing or a high API call limit is your top priority. Choose Hygraph if: you want collaborative features (comments, live preview) and GraphQL on a free tier. title: The Missing Piece in AI Systems
summary: This paper explores the foundational role of humans in effective AI systems’ development. Based on a real-life case study, it examines how people help bridge the gap between technical capability and real-world trust.
body_text: Why Humans Are Still in the Loop Artificial intelligence is transforming how organizations operate, increasingly reducing human involvement. Yet behind the promise of automation lies a growing set of challenges that AI alone cannot solve. Challenges such as bias, reliability, compliance, security, and performance in live environments expose the limits of model-centric approaches. Addressing these issues requires human oversight, contextual understanding, and ongoing intervention. This paper explores the foundational role of humans in effective AI systems’ development. Based on a real-life case study, it examines how people help bridge the gap between technical capability and real-world trust. Designed for business and technology leaders alike, it offers a clear perspective on what it truly takes to build AI systems that perform responsibly, scale sustainably, and deliver lasting value.
